title: A Stone Gone Walking
blurb: A yellow cobble has vanished from Orla's garden row, and Ila's hunt for the thief leads to a confession about Cuthbert and a map with one street at its heart.

blocks.text: Orla Treadgold says good morning to her stones one at a time, the way you'd greet neighbours over a fence, and at first light I follow her down the path with my practice cord in my pocket.
"Morning, Pilchard. Morning, Duchess. Bun." She stops at the row of cobbles along the path. "Mustard?"
Stones don't answer, of course. But there's a hole in the row where a yellow cobble the size of a fist should be, and the hole is full of rain.

Orla crouches and puts two fingers in the water. Behind us the starlings line the fence at their exact intervals, a coin stands on its edge on the potting bench, and the rest of the garden goes on being loud as if nothing has happened.

"Two strands, tied and parked," I say. "And a moved stone takes its knot and its loudness with it, wherever it goes. So somewhere in Brindlemouth there's a stone making coins stand up. And Standards swings these streets."
"It does."
"So anybody with a bob could follow it from the street and work out where it came from." I look at a hundred and forty stones that are each a crime. "Straight back here."
Orla stands. Her knees crack. She doesn't say please. She never says please.
"Find it, Clerk."
It's three weeks since she took me on, three weeks of bare cord and blisters, and this is the first thing she has ever asked me to do for her.

I check the ground first, because a Registry Clerk always checks the ground first. Beside the hole somebody has scooped a handful of gravel off the path. On the terrace steps there's a skid in the clay, on the third one down, the one that rocks.

"The gravel's cover," I say. "If anybody stops him, it's a bag of gravel for a fish tank. And only a knotter would steal a loaded stone, because only a knotter would know it was loaded." I'm already walking. "He went down to Gullet Lane for the first 14 into town. A knotter wants a stone like that on his own bench, where nobody's watching him work it. We're looking for a workshop."
"Are we," says Orla, and follows.

The driver of the first 14 is called Precious. By the chapel I know she has three grandsons and a bad hip, and by the bottom of the hill she knows my dad trues bicycle wheels off Tallow Row. Orla sits at the back with her hands on her knees, watching pigeons.

That's what you watch for. A loud stone isn't a light or a smell. It's small things going exactly right within a hundred metres of it, and none of them hurt anybody: a coin on its edge, birds in a perfect line. So at every stop I put my face to the wet glass and look for something too tidy.
Four stops. Five. At Saddler's Cross there are seven pigeons on the shelter roof, spaced like buttons on a coat.
"This one, Precious, thank you!" I'm off before the doors are all the way open.
Under the shelter a penny lies on its edge in a puddle. I take out my bob and it goes crooked, circles twice and settles. No half-turn. Two.

Mustard is close. I look along the stop for a knotter, and there he is: a man on the bench in a long oilskin, with a rolled leather tool case on his knee, the exact roll a field knotter carries. My heart goes like a tram bell. I'm halfway to him, working out what to say to a man who steals tied knots, when somebody behind me calls out.
"Lucky stones! Twenty p! Lucky stones!"

A boy is sitting on an upturned crate by the timetable, ten or eleven, in a school jumper two sizes too big. On a tea towel in front of him there's a row of washed gravel. And in the middle, yellow and the size of a fist, sits Mustard.

"That one's not twenty p," he says, when he sees me looking. "That's my display one." He flicks a penny onto the pavement. It lands on its edge and stays there. "It makes pennies stand up, miss. It's a good one."
Behind me the man in the oilskin unrolls his leather case. Spanners. He's a plumber.
I look at the penny, and the gravel, and I think of the hole in Orla's row with the rain in it.
"I'm wrong," I say out loud. "Nobody stole a knot. Somebody stole a stone."
Orla, at my shoulder, says nothing, which from Orla is practically a cheer.
I sit down on the kerb beside the crate, because you don't take a thing off somebody before you know their name.
"I'm Ila. What's yours?"
"Robbie."
"Where did you find the good one, Robbie?"

He looks at Orla. Orla looks back. "Up the allotments. My nan's got a plot on the bottom terrace. I went up the top last night and there were pennies standing up all over by the path, so I took the one that was doing it." He swallows. "Is it yours, missus?"
"Mine," says Orla.
"Sorry."

He taps Mustard on the kerb as he says it, just a little nervous tap, and my stomach turns over. A stone that's split or broken is finished as an anchor. Its knot would untie itself right here, and the two strands would fall on whoever signed the docket that tied it. On Orla.
"What's the money for?" I ask, and put my hand gently over the stone.
"My bike's front wheel's buckled. A new one's twelve pound."

"Twelve pounds for a wheel? Robbie, that's robbery." He grins, so I keep going. "My dad trues wheels. The last lock-up off Tallow Row, the one with Brandt painted on the door. Take it round after school and he'll have it running straight by teatime, for nothing. And in exchange, the display one goes home to its garden. Is that fair?"
He thinks about it seriously, the way you should. "Why do pennies stand up round it?"
"I can't tell you, Robbie. I'm not allowed."
"Is it a secret?"
"It's a very boring secret."

He shakes my hand on it. I buy two of the twenty p ones as well, because he's been sitting out here in the rain since seven, and he hands Mustard up to Orla with both hands, like something from church. She puts it in the pocket of her waxed jacket. On the shelter roof the pigeons shuffle and break their line, because the thing that lined them up is leaving.

"Its age stops while it's in your pocket," I tell her on the tram back, because I can't help myself. "It keeps the capacity it had when he lifted it, and it starts ageing again wherever you put it down."
"So it's lost a night," says Orla. "It'll live."
We walk up from Gullet Lane, behind the chapel. On the third step, the one that rocks, Orla stops and stands on it, rocking it, looking down at the estuary.
"You asked me who could shape slack," she says. "I'll tell it once."
I don't say anything. Three weeks has taught me that much.

"Thirty years ago the Corn Exchange came down with Cuthbert inside it. It broke his chest. His heart was going." A long pause. "Its slack was dwelling in the street. Twelve minutes of it. I caught seven strands and tied them into a knot on him that kept his heart catching."
"A knot on a person is legal only under a Sexton's warrant."

"I had no warrant. I had twelve minutes." She shifts on the step. "I tied it as a slip. And I tied a snare to it, so if it ever came undone, its own slack would be shaped into whatever it took to start him again."

"A nurse in the tram queue," I say. "A defibrillator in the shelter. An ambulance already at the lights." And my name on the radio, because I was the keeper. "But knots on people fray. They lose a strand a year, and every lost strand falls on the keeper. A life-knot that falls below the strands it was tied with fails within the season."

"So every year I brought one stone down to the Lantry Steps at noon." She pats her pocket, where Mustard is. "Carried it across the city the way that one went this morning, knot and all. Untied it where I put it down, caught one strand in the dwell and tied it back into his knot where it had frayed. And he walked those steps at noon every day so I'd know where to find him. Thirty years of the same walk at the same hour wore a knot of its own around mine."
"The umbrellas," I whisper. "Two strands."
The half-turn. The half-turn was her. I counted the two outside it, and I untied them, and her seven came loose underneath and stopped his heart.
"I untied your knot."
"You untied the umbrellas," says Orla. "Mine let go because I tied it as a slip. And my snare did what I built it to do." She steps off the rocking stair. "Come on."
"Orla, wait. Slack means an untie. The Corn Exchange was held up by a knot, and somebody untied it. Who?"
"Ask Cuthbert."

Back in the garden she puts Mustard in its hole in the row and presses the soil round it with her thumbs, and says, "There you are," to it, and not to me. Then she holds out her hand for my practice cord.
"Watch."

It's nothing like the drills. Under, over twice, a turn back on itself like a man checking his pocket for his keys, and at the end a loop left open, waiting. There's no slack in the cord. It ties nothing. It's only the shape.
"That's a snare," says Orla. "Every knotter's hands have a signature. Bureau knots are taught from the book and they all look alike. This one isn't in any book. Nobody ties it but me."
"Why are you showing me?"
"So you'll know it." She doesn't say know it where.

So I learn it the way I learned the rulebook, every turn in its place, before I've ever once used it. By the twentieth time my fingers know it the way my mouth knows the rule about dockets. By the thirtieth I can do it with my eyes shut, and Orla grunts, which I am going to treat as praise.
Cuthbert comes up the terrace steps at three, with his brass-cornered case and a flask, and bows to me as if we're at a dance.
"Miss Brandt. I hear you've been recovering stolen property before breakfast, and without so much as a spike."
"Orla told me," I say. "About the slip, and the snare, and a stone at noon every year."
He looks at Orla, and something goes between them that I'm not part of. Then he sits on the bench beside the coin.
"She says to ask you about the Corn Exchange. Slack means an untie. So somebody untied its knot, and the Bureau wrote down—"
"—that I was a credit to the service. Very decent of them." He unscrews the flask. "The Corn Exchange didn't fall, my dear. It was let go."
"Let go by whom? With you inside it?"
He pours tea into the lid of the flask very carefully. "Oh, there's nothing more worth telling," he says, and hums.
I know that hum now. I don't push. I drink the tea he passes me and I watch Orla not looking at him.
Dad's lock-up smells of oil and wet rubber. When I get there at eight, a small bicycle is leaning by the door with a front wheel as straight as a ruler.
"Your friend came," Dad says, without looking up from the hub between his knees. "Robbie. Said you'd sent him."
"Did you mind?"
"It was a good rim." He spins the hub. "Next time, ask, Inspector."
"Can I borrow your chalk? And the back wall?"
He hands me the fat yellow chalk he marks tyres with and asks nothing at all, which is the kindest thing anyone has done for me today.

The wall is whitewashed brick. I draw Brindlemouth on it from memory: the estuary, the docks, Tallow Row, the lines of the trams. My supervisor boxed up my two hundred and twelve copies and took them away. But I copied every one of them out in my own hand, and I remember them the way I remember the rules. Address by address, I put them back.
A few dots by the docks. A ring round the old market. A scatter up by the bridges. Thin, all of them, next to the one I'm drawing now.

Missed trams. Missed buses. A job interview missed by a minute. A wedding where the bride's own mother came in after the vows. Again and again, the same streets, and at the bottom of every one the same stamp: Site swung, no knot found. No Action.
Of course no knot was found. Nobody swung a person.

The dots crowd together until the chalk is a smudge, and in the middle of the smudge is one street, Hobday Street. And I remember, word for word, a complaint I copied two winters ago from a woman on Hobday Street: I have missed the 14 every morning this month by one second, and every morning the lad from number nine in the Same-Day jacket catches it, whistling.
I put the chalk down. Brindlemouth Same-Day. Eastern Round. Never late in his life.
The thickest cluster in four years of complaints is drawn round one front door, and it's Ferdie Lusk's.
